trials.title: macOS 27: first bootstrap of a LaunchAgent -- process identity and BTM registration
macOS 27: external launchctl bootout -- children with no detach / Setpgid / Setsid
macOS 27: launchctl kickstart -k -- children with no detach / Setpgid / Setsid
trials.changes: Same harness; job re-bootstrapped and left running 11s (past the 10s throttle window), three idle children spawned (nil / Setpgid / Setsid SysProcAttr, SIGTERM ignored+logged), then `launchctl kickstart -k gui/501/<label>` from a terminal.
trials.expected: Setpgid and Setsid children get no signal and survive (90%); no-detach child gets the group SIGTERM at main-process exit (85%); immediate respawn (80%); 55% that -k sends SIGTERM rather than SIGKILL.
trials.actual: kickstart -k sent SIGTERM (daemon logged "signal terminated" 9ms after the call); new instance started 30ms later and answered /healthz 104ms after the kickstart call. No-detach child got SIGTERM 8ms after the daemon (group kill) and survived only by ignoring it; Setpgid and Setsid children received nothing, reparented to pid 1, ran to their natural end 11s later.

trials.title: macOS 27: kill -9 of the service's main process -- children with no detach / Setpgid / Setsid
trials.changes: Same harness; job had run >10s; three idle children spawned (nil / Setpgid / Setsid, SIGTERM ignored+logged); `kill -9 <job pid>` from a terminal; KeepAlive=true in the plist.
trials.expected: KeepAlive respawns at once (ran > ThrottleInterval) (80%); no-detach child gets the group SIGTERM when launchd reaps the main process (85%); Setpgid/Setsid untouched (90%).
trials.actual: Respawned 31ms after the SIGKILL, healthy at 87ms. No-detach child got SIGTERM 6ms after the kill (launchd's group kill on job exit), survived only by ignoring it. Setpgid and Setsid children got nothing, reparented to pid 1, finished normally 13s later.

macOS 27: BTM re-walk -> "updated item" for every adhoc build, even with a stable codesign identifier
macOS 27: a stable self-signed certificate does not keep BTM's LWCR -- only Team-ID (Developer ID) signing avoids the per-update notice
trials.changes: Temporary keychain (deleted afterwards; login search list restored at once) with a self-signed codeSigning certificate "Seamless Spike Test Signing" (CSSMERR_TP_NOT_TRUSTED). v7 and v8 (different bytes) signed `codesign -s <sha1> --keychain <tmp> -f -i org.thereisnospoon.spiked`; both designated requirements identical: `identifier "org.thereisnospoon.spiked" and certificate leaf = H"26967222..."`, TeamIdentifier not set. Each: swap, bootout/bootstrap, touch-triggered BTM re-walk.
trials.expected: launchd runs an untrusted-cert binary (75%). v7->v8 logged "updated item with same LWCR" (40%) vs "updated item" (60%, if BTM keys on TeamIdentifier).
trials.actual: Both ran under launchd (spawned, healthy; no Launch Constraint lines). B3 (adhoc -> cert): `updated item: uuid=45AD3646...`. B4 (same cert, new bytes, identical designated requirement): `updated item: uuid=0AB9CEE3...` -- a NEW LWCR again, not "with same LWCR". […] Conclusion: for legacy LaunchAgents BTM's LWCR follows the Team ID; anything without one (adhoc, adhoc+identifier, self-signed) is a new background item per build -> a "Background Items Added" notice per update. Avoiding it needs Developer ID signing of the darwin binaries (e.g. rcodesign in the release workflow).

Windows 11 (26200): a Task Scheduler-launched daemon is in a shared job with only SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK
Windows 11: Stop-ScheduledTask ends only the task's process -- children of every creation-flag kind survive (S4U task)
Windows 11: schtasks /End and taskkill /F of the daemon also leave every child alive (S4U task)
Windows 11: per-user on-demand update task registers and runs fine, but an immediate Stop+Start of the service task left it DOWN
Windows 11: schtasks /End returns ~1.1s before the task's process exits -- an immediate /Run races the old listener (seamlessd's restart verb)
trials.changes: Harness w3 (logs any console control event: os.Interrupt / SIGTERM). Four restarts of \SeamlessSpike (S4U) exactly as cmd/seamlessd/service.go's actionRestart does on Windows: `schtasks /End` then `schtasks /Run` immediately (runs 1, 3), vs `/End`, poll the old process until HasExited, then `/Run` (runs 2, 4). Health polled with Invoke-WebRequest.
trials.expected: /End returns ~0.1s; the old process lingers ~1s; immediate /Run -> bind failure and a dead task (85%); no console control event, a plain terminate (60%); the wait arm healthy ~1.6s after /End (80%).
trials.actual: /End returned in 0.035-0.16s every time; the old process actually exited 1.064s / 1.182s after /End (wait arm). No "signal" line in the daemon log in any run: Task Scheduler sent no CTRL_C/CTRL_CLOSE -- a hard terminate ~1.1s after the stop request, so a daemon gets no graceful shutdown. Immediate arm: run 1 got lucky (new instance listened, healthy +5.4s), run 3 lost the race (`bind: Only one usage of each socket address`, task Ready, lastResult 0x1, still down 25s later). Wait arm: healthy +2.18s and +3.86s after /End (~1.1s exit wait + ~0.6s start + PS 5.1 polling overhead). => `seamlessd restart` (and the updater's rollback/restart via serviceControl) on Windows can leave the daemon down until next logon; it must wait for the old serve process to exit before /Run, as install.ps1's Stop-Daemon (Stop-Process + Wait-Process) already does.

Linux Ubuntu 24.04: identity of the daemon inside the installer's seamless.service unit (cgroup v2, systemd 255)
Linux Ubuntu 24.04: plain and Setsid children of the daemon are SIGTERMed with it on restart AND stop, then SIGKILLed at the 90s stop timeout
trials.changes: Mock daemon in the installer-shaped seamless.service spawned two idle updaters via exec.Command + go Wait (stdio = a file): SysProcAttr nil (plain) and {Setsid:true}. Both log and IGNORE SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGCONT and write a heartbeat file every 250ms. Then (run 1) `systemctl --user restart seamless.service`, (run 2) a fresh pair and `systemctl --user stop seamless.service`, both timed from the shell; user-manager journal read with sudo.
trials.expected: Both children get SIGTERM in the same instant as the daemon (95%: KillMode=control-group signals the whole cgroup); because they ignore SIGTERM, the restart blocks until TimeoutStopSec (90s default) then SIGKILL (85%); Setsid makes no difference (95%); stop identical (95%).
trials.actual: As predicted, both runs. systemd-cgls before: both updaters inside /user.slice/user-501.slice/user@501.service/app.slice/seamless.service (the Setsid one with pgid=sid=its pid, the plain one in the daemon's pgid 1321). Restart at 23:20:15.683: daemon, plain and Setsid child all got SIGTERM+SIGCONT within 0.6ms (15.6873-15.6879); the daemon exited at +62ms; both children got a SECOND SIGTERM+SIGCONT (state final-sigterm) and were reparented to the user manager (988). `systemctl --user restart` returned after 90.16s: journal "seamless.service: State 'final-sigterm' timed out. Killing." / "Killing process 1377 (seamlessd) with signal SIGKILL." / "Killing process 1390 ..." / "Failed with result 'timeout'." / "Found left-over process 1390 (seamlessd) in control group while starting unit. Ignoring.", then "Started seamless.service" and a new instance at 23:21:45.846. Heartbeats stopped at the SIGKILL. Stop: identical (deactivating (final-sigterm) for 90.12s, SIGKILL to both). A real updater with Go's default SIGTERM handling would die at the installer's first `systemctl --user restart`, mid-install.

Linux Arch (systemd 261): a transient updater's restart hit seamless.service's start limit in a realistic sequence -- the installer-style `systemctl --user restart` fails and the daemon stays DOWN
trials.changes: Unplanned, observed during the Arch distro-test.sh run: seamless.service was enabled by an earlier aborted run, so the login started it (start 1), then setup.sh's restart (2), item b's restart (3), item c's restart (4), item c's stop+start (5) -- all within ~6s -- and then a transient updater (systemd-run --user --unit=seamless-update-<ULID>, running the installer stand-in: show-environment, daemon-reload, restart) restarted it (6).
trials.expected: (Not predicted: the start-limit trial on Ubuntu 24.04 had shown the mechanism, but this sequence was expected to stay under it.)
trials.actual: 23:55:33.511 user manager: "seamless.service: Start request repeated too quickly." / "Failed with result 'start-limit-hit'."; the stand-in's `systemctl --user restart` rc=1 with systemd 261's text: "Job for seamless.service failed because start of the service was attempted too often. See \"systemctl --user status seamless.service\" and \"journalctl --user -xeu seamless.service\" for details. To force a start use \"systemctl --user reset-failed seamless.service\" followed by \"systemctl --user start seamless.service\" again." The daemon stayed down (the next spawn request got "connection refused") until an unrelated `systemctl --user restart` 5.1s later, after the 10s window -- Restart=always never restarts a start-limit-hit unit. Five starts in 10s is the default burst (StartLimitIntervalUSec=10s, StartLimitBurst=5 on every distro measured; the installer's unit sets neither). A normal single update is 1 start, but an installer restart plus an updater verification/rollback restart plus an owner's restarts can reach it; an updater that sees this must `systemctl --user reset-failed seamless.service` and start again (or wait out the window), and should never treat a failed restart as "the old daemon is still serving".
